name: Park Place Apartments
headline: Evergreen Real Estate Group plans a new five-story building at 1275 Decatur St. in Denver's Sun Valley neighborhood with 80 three- and four-bedroom apartments for households at 80% to 120% AMI. It won $1,640,026 in Colorado's first round of Middle-Income Housing Tax Credits.
why_it_matters: It is one of the first three MIHTC awards and tests whether a family-sized, middle-income building can be financed with only the state credit, private equity and a HUD-insured loan, with no local soft money. As of October 2026 the land purchase and building permit are still not on public record.

status.label: Credits awarded; land purchase, site plan approval and permits not confirmed
status.detail: CHFA listed the award as of 2025-07-21. A concept plan was reported in January 2026. In February 2026 the developer said it was under contract to buy the site from the Lions and expected to close in December, with construction by early 2027. Denver's open permit data, updated through 2026-10-19, shows no construction or demolition permit for 1275 Decatur St.

next_step: Watch for the land closing (a deed from the Lions to an Evergreen entity, expected December 2026), a Site Development Plan approval, and demolition and building permits for 1275 Decatur St. in Denver's permit data.

key_numbers.meaning: All units are income-restricted, with 20 each at 80%, 90%, 100% and 120% AMI.
The applicant calls this an annual allocation. MIHTC is a five-year state credit claimed ratably, so the total is about $8.2M over five years (inferred).
BusinessDen's figure. The application gives a total development cost of $499,123 per unit, or about $39.9M (inferred), with construction at $330,747 per unit.
The applicant committed to 20 years, beyond the program's 15-year minimum.

facts.value: 1275 Decatur St., Denver, in the Sun Valley neighborhood near Federal Boulevard and Holden Place, next to Rude Park and the Rude Recreation Center
I/F, N: individuals and families, new construction
About 34,100 sq ft (reported as 0.8 acre), zoned C-MX-5. The applicant says no rezoning or variances are needed
Five stories, about 70 feet. All units face a central landscaped courtyard with a playground. There are 64 at-grade, screened (tuck-under) parking spaces
BusinessDen put 80% to 120% AMI at $93,800 to $151,320 for a family of three and $104,200 to $168,120 for a family of four
0.1 mile from the Decatur-Federal W Line light rail station, and next to a bus stop on RTD routes 15L and 16
All-electric, with cold-climate heat pumps and heat pump water heaters. It targets NGBS Silver certification, has EV-ready parking for 10% of spaces, and is solar ready
Rude Park Apartments, on CHFA's March 2025 MIHTC letters-of-intent report

money.note: The applicant calls it annual. It is a five-year credit claimed ratably. The March 2025 LOI asked for $1,650,000, and the May 2025 applicant report shows $1,640,455.
Clocktower Tax Credits, LLC. The investor gets only the credit, with no cash flow, depreciation or sale proceeds.
Weave Social Finance, a Denver-based mixed-income housing fund. It shares in cash flow, depreciation and sale proceeds.
To be originated by KeyBank, plus a supplemental construction-only loan from KeyBank. The application said debt terms were still in discussion.

money.source: CHFA Middle Income Access Program (MIAP) subordinate debt
money.note: Planned as subordinate debt after stabilization.
The applicant says the project uses no soft funds or grants.

parties.name: Evergreen Real Estate Group (Chicago-based, with a Denver office)
Evergreen Real Estate Services, LLC (Evergreen's management company)
Clocktower Tax Credits, LLC (MIHTC) and Weave Social Finance, LLC (private equity)
Denver Lions Foundation / Lions Club of Denver, owner since 1959

background.text: The site holds the former Lions Rude Park learning center building. The Lions owned it from 1959 and had planned to replace it with a new daycare. They dropped that plan when the cost estimate rose from about $3.5M to $9.5M to $10M.

The Denver Lions Early Learning Center nonprofit dissolved, and the Denver Lions Foundation took over its assets and liabilities on 2025-01-01. A late-2024 member survey favored selling the building. The foundation then moved to negotiate a letter of intent for exclusive good-faith sale talks with Evergreen. The LOI did not oblige it to sell.

Evergreen was picked after the Lions issued a public request for a developer. The application says Evergreen has full site control through an executed purchase and sale agreement. At the Lions' request, outreach was held back until that agreement was signed. The price is not public.

The application reports a Phase I environmental assessment with no recognized environmental conditions and a completed NEPA Part 58 checklist. It planned a Site Development Plan submittal in Q4 2025 and a building permit within 180 days of that submittal.
Naked Denver reported a concept plan for the project on 2026-01-23. BusinessDen reported that Evergreen filed the proposal with the city in January 2026.

The ground floor holds a lobby, coworking space, fitness center, pet wash, bike parking and management offices. Units have in-unit washers and dryers. Open-air corridors and a naturally ventilated garage are used to save on cost and energy, and the exterior is mostly stucco.

The applicant's market study (JRES) counts more than 1,950 income-qualified households in the market area and a 5.3% capture rate. It notes that four-bedroom units are only 0.5% of metro Denver's apartment stock.
Park Place was one of three projects in CHFA's first MIHTC round, which awarded about $4.8M in credits for 220 units. CHFA received 12 letters of intent and five applications in that round.
No project-based vouchers or other rental subsidy are mentioned in any source.

discrepancies.text: The application narrative says the project requested $1,650,000 a year in MIHTC, but CHFA's applicant report lists the request as $1,640,455.
CHFA's award is $1,640,026, while Bisnow and Hoodline report about $1.65 million.

The application and Bisnow call the existing structure a commercial building, and BusinessDen and Hoodline call it a vacant school building. Naked Denver and the Lions say a Montessori preschool (Mile High Learning) operated in it.
In December 2025 Bisnow reported a construction start in fall 2026. In February 2026 BusinessDen reported a start by early 2027.
Naked Denver and the Lions' own page name the owner as the Denver Lions Foundation, while BusinessDen and Hoodline name the Lions Club of Denver.

open_questions: Whether the land purchase closed, at what price, and into which ownership entity.
Site Development Plan number, status and approval date. No city record was found; only press reports of a concept plan.

Whether demolition and building permits have been filed. None appear in Denver's open permit data through 2026-10-19.
